ANNUAL REPORT 
YOUNG MEN’S CHRISTIAN 
ASSOCIATION 


ORGANIZED INCORPORATED 


Nov., 1851. Dec ,, 1870. 


OF THE CITY OF MONTREAL. 


PRESENTED AT THE ANNUAL MEETING HELD ON TUESDAY EVENING 
MAY 19TH, 1903. 


MONTREAL : 
‘““WITNESS ” PRINTING HOUSE. 


1903. 


Loy 


ANNUAL MEETING, 


The Fifty-Second Annual Meeting of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association was held on Tuesday evening, May 
1th, 1908, at 8.15 o’clock. 

Mr. Robert Munro, president, occupied the chair. The 
Chairman read the 72nd Psalm. Prayer was offered by 
Mir. R. L. Charlton. The minutes of the previous meeting 
were accepted as read. 

The Secretary then read the 52nd Annual Report of 
the Board of Directors. 

The financial statement of the Association was pre- 
sented by Mr. L. H. Packard, Treasurer. 

Mr. C. T. Williams presented the report of the Com- 
mittee on Vacancies, nominating the following Directors 
for the next three years :— 


L. H. Packard. Dr. Wm. F. Hamilton. GC. W. Brown 
S. P. Leet. John W. Ross. W.S. Leslie. 
G. F. Johnston. 


No other nominations having been presented by the 
members of the Association, according to the Constitu- 
tion, on motion of Mr. Williams the Secretary was. re- 
quested to cast one ballot on behalf of the above list of 
names, the President declared them elected. 

The detailed reports of the various committees, in- 
stead of being read as on former years, was presented by 
means of lantern slides. Mr. C. K. Calhoun, Assistant 
Secretary, made the presentation. Seventy-five slides re- 
viewing all the departments of the work were used. 

Mr. D. W. Ross supported the report of the Board of 
Directors in reference to the Forward Movement for an 
enlarged work in the city. 

Moved by Mr. Ross, seconded by Mr. Geo. E. Williams, 
that the above reports as presented be adopted and sub- 
mitted to the Committee for printing and circulating 
among the members and subscribers of the Association. 

Moved by Mr. Jas. R. Greig, seconded by Mr. L. H. 
Packard, that the thanks of the Association be tendered 
to the press, citizens and ladies for the service they had 
all rendered to this work during the past year. 

The meeting then adjourned.

The Board of Directors earnestly solicit Gifts and Bequests towards 
the extension of this important work for the men and boys of the city. 


ANNUAL REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS. 


In presenting the detailed reports of the year’s work 
which closed April 30th, the Board of Directors are deep- 
ly grateful for the results which have been realized. 


Directors’ Meetings. 


Your directors have had the whole work under careful 
review in their monthly business meetings, and have also 
maintained a meeting each Friday morning for united 
petition to God for His guidance and the bestowment of 
His blessing upon the whole work. 


The Staff. 


Your directors are pleased to bear testimony to the 
self-denial, loyalty and efficiency of the members of the 
staff, and their devotion to the interests of the Associa- 
tion. The supervision of the various departments has 
been greatly strengthened by means of the Conference of 
the members of the staff held each week. Unity of aim 
and effort has been secured and the forces directed to 
better purpose. Never has the welfare of the individual 
member had more careful consideration. 


Dominion Square Building. 


The use of the Central Building has been greater than 
any year since its opening, and your directors are com- 
pelled to consider the question of enlargement if they are 
to meet the pressing demands of the physical, educational 
and boys’ departments. Without immediate enlargement 
they cannot hope to do more than “mark time” in these 
important branches. 


Constitution. 
Your directors have had the Constitution of the Asso- 
ciation under careful revision. The changed conditions 


of the Association work rendered this necessary. On 
January 28th a special meeting of members was called 


i4 


and the proposed Constitution was submitted. Notice 
of motion was given that in three months this Constitu- 
tion would be submitted to the Association for consider- 
ation and adoption. On Tuesday evening, April 28th, a 
special meeting was called for this purpose, and the 
revised Constitution submitted and adopted. This will 
now be printed in the Annual Report, and the directors 
call the attention of all members to this important docu- 
ment. 


Membership. 


The total membership on April 30th was 2,177, being 
a gain of 62 over last year, notwithstanding the loss of 72 
members on account of the closing of educational classes 
to business boys, and through lack of accommodation. 

The receipts from members and tuition fees amounted 
to $9,275.75, a gain of $283.00 over last year. Five years 
ago the receipts from the same source were $6,146, show- 
ing a gain of fully fifty percent. The fixing of a standard 
fee of $2.00 for membership and then making an added 
charge for the privileges of the various departments as 
required, is considered the most satisfactory basis on 
which to place the fees. This will, doubtless, be the future 
policy of the Association. 


Finances. 


The finances have received most careful consideration. 
The treasurer’s statement shows a slight increase both 
from members’ fees and rentals. Subscriptions have not 
been quite as large as estimated. A healthy work must 
be constantly growing and this demands enlarged expen- 
diture. An increased income is available from three 
sources: A larger membership enlisting new business 
firms and citizens and securing from our interested mem- 
bers who appreciate the value of the Association, a sub- 
cription in addition to their members’ fee. This should 
have the continued attention of the finance and member- 
ship committees. 

Since entering upon this building each annual state- 
ment has been presented with all the bills paid. This year 
is no exception. The directors are thankful to the mem- 
bers and»to the business men and other friends for this 
result. 


Religious Work. 


The religious work shows a decided gain in the attend- 
ance at the Men’s Meetings, an increase of from four to 
six in the number of Bible classes held each week, and 
also an encouraging increase in the results secured. One 
hundred and eighty young men expressed a desire to lead 
the christian life. Of this number 146 names and parti- 
culars were sent to city pastors, also the names of 76 
other young men who had recently come to the city. Thus 
222 young men were introduced directly to city churches 
during the year. In all departments of the Association 
the aim to help men spiritually has been emphasized, and 
a very large amount of work done in personal visitation 
and counsel with young men, in visitation of the sick and 
in correspondence which cannot possibly be recorded. 
The future policy should be to strengthen the Men’s Meet- 
ing by securing the ablest possible speakers on these 
great questions of the religious life, and also increase the 
number of group classes for Bible study. Religious work 
for men should also be undertaken at points outside the 
building. The Religious Work Department presents a 
field of the greatest possible opportunity and promise, 
and much larger results both for the Association and the 
churches of our city might be secured if it was possible 
to devote the entire time of one member of the staff to 
the work of this department. 


Evening Classes. 


The Educational Department shows an addition of 
three subjects in the study courses ; an enrolment of 436 
different members, being an increase of 77 over last year; 
100 more men were held through the whole term of six 
months, and an increase of $563.00 paid in tuition fees. 
The Literary Society had a most successful season. 
The Committee has set an aim to secure six hundred dif- 
ferent men in evening class studies next fall. They are 
also considering the addition of a spring term. <A “ Ca- 
nadian Club” has been formed for the study and discus- 
sion of Canadian questions. 

An Endowment Fund is greatly needed for the super- 
vision and development of this most important agency. 


Physical Work. 


The Gymnasium class registration was 654, an in- 
crease of 23 over last year. At least 250 members take 
exercise apart from the regular classes. The use of the 
bathing facilities has never been so large as the past 
year. From October to January it was necessary to keep 
a “ waiting list ” for lockers of from twenty to fifty mem- 
bers. This proved a serious hindrance to the class work. 
Increased locker accommodation, including a separate 
locker room for business men is an absolute necessity. 

The growth of the various clubs—now eight in num- 
ber—is most encouraging. But the outlook is dark for 
this season on account of the difficulty of securing suit- 
able grounds. Your directors would record their appre- 
ciation of the excellent service rendered by the Leaders’ 
Corps. The continued success of the Gymnasium Men’s 
Bible Study Club has had an important bearing on the 
general good-fellowship which has prevailed amongst the 
men using the Physical Department. 


The Boys’ Work. 


The work for boys has been continued at the Central 
Building, and also at the North East End, and at Point 
St. Charles. Fifty-three boys served on committees, and 
forty-seven graduated into the Senior Department. Re- 
ligious meetings were conducted at all these points, and 
seven group Bible classes were held during last fall and 
winter. The evening classes for business boys had to be 
discontinued for lack of room. The gymnasium class 
work was well sustained, as was also the social features 
of the work. The North East Branch was very carefully 
supervised by the committee in charge at great sacrifice 
and self-denial to the members 

The urgent need is for a separate annex, where this 
work could be carried on without its present limitations 
and restrictions. |Your directors hope this will soon be 
realized. 


Employment. 


The large number of young men who are now coming 
to Canada from Great Britain has greatly increased the 
work of the Employment Bureau. <A considerable num- 


17 


ber remain in the city, but the majority go farther west. 
Counselling with these men as to where to locate, etc., is 
most important. Our own members, in an increasing 
number, are looking to the Association for counsel and 
co-operation regarding employment. The time of one 
man for one half of each day is required for this work. 


Summer Camp. 

The Camp at Lac St. Joseph, Ste. Agathe, had its best 
season last summer. Two hundred and ten men and boys 
spent a delightful vacation there. This is a most helpful 
branch of the work, and care should be taken to keep the 
equipment in the best possible condition and have the 
most careful supervision. 


Railway Branch, 

The efforts of the directors have been centered in 
securing a suitable building for this branch at Point St. 
Charles. They are pleased to report that through the co- 
operation of the Grand Trunk Railway Management, this 
is now almost accomplished. A much larger building, 
with better equipment than was at first thought possible, 
is now assured. It is expected to be open about October 
ist. When completed it will cost $40,000. Of this amount 
the site and $15,000 have been donated by the Railway. 
This Association has become responsible for $15,000 and 
collections are now in progress amongst the employees 
of the Company and the residents at Point St. Charles 
for the balance. Your directors confidently expect that 
this building will be an important factor in the work. for 
the young men of that large and crowded section of the 
city. 


Association Bulletin. 


So large and varied are the activities of the Associa- 
tion as to render necessary the issue of a weekly or 
monthly bulletin so as to keep members, subscribers and 
friends in touch with the progress of the work.  Provi- 
sion should be made for such a publication, to begin not 
later than September 1st. 


A Forward Movement. 


Among the organizations of the day which have for 
their object the betterment of men, the Young Men’s 


18 


Christian Association stands easily in the fore-front. It 
has not only a provincial and continental, but a world- 
wide influence. Its growth is phenomenal. Its solid 
foundation, the stability of its management, its high 
ideals, and its practical work, insure for it a yet more 
prominent place in the city, town and country life of our 
land. Because it deals with youth it deals with the 
future. No investment can possibly be more profitable 
than that placed on young manhood. Business men real: 
ize this as never before. During the past year one manu- 
facturing concern of Indiana, desiring to mark their fifty 
years in business by a fitting memorial, gave $200,000 to 
the Association in their city for a new building and 
equipment. The following facts for the year 1902 are 
startling as to the growth of the movement on this con- 
tinent : 

Twenty-four City Association Buildings completed at 
a cost of $1,304,000. 

Additions and improvements to fourteen Buildings at 
a cost of $216,900. 

Twenty-nine Buildings now in process of erection, to 
cost $2,674,500. 

Amounts pledged for prospective Buildings at forty- 
three points, $1,110,200. 

For College Buildings, at six points, $347,000. 

For Railroad Buildings, at thirty-one points, either 
erected last year or assured, $525,000. 

For Boys’ Department Buildings, at four points, 
$125,000. 


These facts need no comment. Business men appre- 
ciate this opportunity. Has any man who placed $100 or 
$1,000 in our Dominion Square Building ever regretted 
his investment ? It has yielded large returns. Twelve 
years have passed since it was opened. Reports in all 
the departments indicate the need of enlargement. 

The following represent the immediate and absolute 
needs of the Association. 

First: An Annex to our Building for the Boys’ De. 
partment, including an. up-to-date equipment. The work 
for boys may ere long become the most important depart: 
ment of the Association. Formerly it was confined to 
school boys, now it has entered the field for the great 
mass of business boys, from fourteen to eighteen years 


1S, 


of age. To do efficient work for this important class, a 
separate equipment on physical, and educational, as well 
as social and religious lines is needed. 

Second : The extension of our Gymnasium and Locker 
Room facilities and the enlargement of our Educational 
Class Rooms and equipment for men. This will include 
added dormitories for members. 

Third : A Branch Building in the North East End of 
the city, suitably equipped for work for boys. Two years’ 
experience in rented quarters in this locality convinces 
the directors that there is both a great need and a great 
opportunity here. This district contains a large Protes- 
tant population, which is rapidly increasing, as is evi 
denced by the fact that the two largest Protestant 
schools in the city are situated in it. There is no ade- 
quate provision for the great mass of boys in this section. 
It is impossible to secure suitable rented quarters. 

Fourth : An Athletic Field, in order to provide facil- 
ities for the large number of men and boys on our mem- 
bership, who are urgently calling for suitable grounds for 
athletic purposes. 

Fifth: A Branch Building for Westmount, similar 
to the one in the North East End, suitably equipped for a 
work for boys. 

With such an enlarged equipment at the Central 
Building we could provide for four thousand members 
without increasing the current expenses more than fifty 
percent. Our location is ideal, in the centre of the board: 
ing house district, adjacent to the railway depots, and of 
easy access from all sections of the city by street cars. A 
conservative estimate of the amount required to supply 
these needs is 


ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE THOUSAND DOLLARS. 


After the most thorough and careful consideration of 
this whole matter, your directors endorse this extension 
movement, and confidently make this appeal to the mem- 
bers, business men, citizens and friends of young men and 
boys in this city. As the money is subscribed the work 
will be undertaken. The need is so urgent that both the 
Annex to the Central Building and the North East 
Branch should be started this fall so as to be ready for 
occupation not later than September, 1904. 


20 


Gifts and subscriptions toward this extension move- 
ment are now earnestly solicited. 


A PERMANENT FUND. 


In addition to these needs, the Association should 
have a Permanent Fund created, the interest from which 
could be devoted towards the maintainance of particular 
branches of the work. For instance: the Association 
Library ; the supervision and development of the Educa- 
tional Work ; the Religious Work, the Work for Boys. 
No large educational work in a community can be effec 
tively sustained without such a permanent fund. There- 
fore, the directors invite contributions towards such a 
Permanent Fund.

reduction of the fee of those entering the Educational 
Classes from $5.00 to $2.00 made the work of the Com- 
mittee more difficult in keeping up the receipts. On April 
80th the membership stood as follows :—

REPORTS OF COMMITTEES. 


RELIGIOUS DEPARTMENT. 


The work of this department has been carried on with 
increased interest during the past year. We are greatly 
indebted to the visit of Mr. Fred B. Smith, of the Inter- 
national Committee, Oct. 31 to Noy. 2, for enlarged plans 
and a new view of our opportunities and responsibilities. 

This Committee was reorganized in November and 
has met regularly since. It is composed of the chairmen 
of the various meetings and Bible classes. Immediately 
growing out of this reorganization was the adoption of 
larger plans for the Sunday afternoon men’s meeting. It 
was late in the fall when arrangements were undertaken, 
consequently not as much progress was made as was 
hoped for, but sufficient to greatly encourage the Com- 
mittee. Strong speakers from other cities as well as from 
our own were secured. The music was made attractive 
by the services of the Male Quartette and the orchestra. 
In January the meetings were taken to the large hall, 
where they were continued until April 26th. Two mass 
meetings for men were held in St. James Church, address- 
ed by Mr. Fred. B. Smith and Mr. Robert E. Speer. The 
attendance at these being fifteen hundred and twelve 
hundred respectively. Throughout the season the main 
evangelistic purpose of the meetings was kept prominent 
and the Committee rejoices to believe that scores of men 
are now serving Jesus Christ who were brought to a deci- 
sion through this agency. While the attendance has 
more than doubled over the previous year the Committee 
look upon it as only a good start. Correspondence is 
already in progress with speakers for next season and it 
is hoped to enlarge and perfect the organization of work- 
ers. 

The Saturday night meeting has continued during the 
year with a total attendance of 2,968, average, 58, a de- 
crease of four over the previous year. Meetings of special 
interest were held on Sept. 26th, when Messrs. Phelps, 
Harvey, Murray and Carter, secretaries of the Inter- 
national Committee, en route to the foreign field, were 


29 


present and spoke. Nov. Ist when Mr. Fred. B. Smith 
spoke and April 11th, when Mr. Robert E. Speer was the 
speaker. The meetings have been helpful to the Chris- 
tian life of many, and the personal invitation which has 
peen extended at almost every meeting has found fre- 
quent response from those who were desirous of begin- 
ning the Christian life.

Service has been conducted at the Western Hospital 
every Sunday morning during the year by the Committee 
in charge. The patients look forward to the service and 
invariably express their appreciation. The thanks of the 
Committee are due to a number of ladies of Erskine, 
Westmount Methodist, Emmanuel and other churches 
who have rendered valuable assistance. An enjoyable 
programme was also provided for the Christmas Tree. 


Sunday Afternoon Bible Class, 


The total attendance for the year was 3,235, am aver- 
age of 63 per Sunday, an increased average of three over 
the previous year. From May to September we continued 
our studies in the Gospel of St. John, and in October com- 
menced with “Lessons from Old Testament Characters 
and Jewish History.” These studies have been very [TO 
fitable, At each meeting note has been taken of any 
strangers present and a letter has been mailed to them 
during the week, inviting them to become regular mem- 
bers of the class. Personal calls have been made, and 
letters sent, from time to time, to absent and sick mem- 


30 


bers. As in former years, a number of our members haye 
taken up Sunday-school work, and others have gone to 
reside in distant parts of the country. In response to the 
kind invitation of Mr. and Mrs. Budge to an “ At Home ” 
in the Association parlors on Noy. 28th, a very pleasant 
evening was enjoyed. A special Christmas service was 
held on Dec. 2ist, attendance, 102. In February the mem- 
bers of the class had a sleigh drive, returning to the 
Association for refreshments. The treasurer reports all 
accounts paid with a small balance on hand. ‘The class 
greatly appreciates the faithful ‘services of our beloved 
leader, Mr. Budge, Mr. W. T. Walmsley, organist, and Mr. 
Harry Griffiths ,leader of the singing. 

The testimony from members as to the influence of 
the class in bringing them to the Saviour and saving 
them from the power of sin, has been most encouraging. 


Gymnasium Men’s Bible Study Club. 


The Gymnasium Men’s Bible Study Club continued, 
under the leadership of Mr. J. E. Merritt, physical direc- 
tor. This class held thirty sessions from September to 
May, with an average attendance of 37, an increase of 
five over last year. The interest in the studies has been 
well sustained, and the class is now past the experi- 
mental stage and will be a permanent feature of our 
Bible study work. It has had a most gratifying influence 
upon the entire Physical Department. 


Evening Class—-Men’s Bible Studies. 


A new feature this year was the organization of a 
Bible class in the Educational Department, under the 
leadership of Mr. Harry Ballantyne, especially to interest 
members of the evening classes. Twenty-five sessions 
were held with a total attendance of 285, average 11. 

We are indebted to Rey. J. L. Gilmour, who has con- 
ducted a Bible class on Tuesday evenings, studying “Old 
Testament Characters.” While the attendance has not 
been large the studies have been exceedingly profitable. 

Two other classes met on Tuesday evenings. One 
conducted by Mr. D. A. Budge, studying “The Life of 
Christ,” and the other, by Mr. C. K. Calhoun, studying a 
normal course in “The Teaching of Bible Classes.” 

Special attention has been given to the following up 


31 


ot enquirers. We have the names of over one hundred 
and eighty men who expressed their purpose to live a 
Christian life. One hundred and forty-six of these names 
were sent by personal letter to pastors, and, in addition, 
seventy-six names of other young men were referred to 
pastors for visitation, etc. We are glad to report that 
thirty-one young men, that we know of, have united with 
the churches in this city whom we believe were influ- 
enced to this step by the Association. Forty-three 
churches of the city and suburbs were interested in these 
results. 


SOCIAL DEPARTMENT. 


The work of the Social Committee was undertaken on 
somewhat different lines this year, and social work in 
the Educational, Physical and Religious Departments 
has. been conducted through the committees in charge of 
those departments rather than by the Social Committee 
direct. It was felt that in this way the talents of the 
members in those departments could be used to better 
advantage, and that the responsibility for a healthy 
social life should rest, in part, upon the Department 
Committees of the Association. As a result several inter- 
class socials have been held both in the Educational and 
Physical Departments, and also two social features in 
connection with the Bible Study Department. 

In addition to the foregoing a very enjoyable parlor 
social was held on Thursday evening, Sept. 11th. 

The attendance at the New Year’s reception was large 
and gratifying, aggregating about 2,500 people. Members 
of the Board of Directors assisted the Reception Com- 
mittee in receiving our friends on that afternoon. An 
interesting programme was carried out in the gymna- 
sium. Two illustrated lectures were given, one the 
“Bickmore Views of British Columbia and Alberta,” by 
Dr. F. W. Kelley, of the High School ; the other “ Beyond 
the Clearings,” descriptive of the wilds of northern and 
north-western Canada, by Mr. Chas. A. Bramble. The 
concert in Association Hall was no exception to former 
years. Several fine loans of pictures and a _ beautiful 
collection of eastern photographs, loaned by Mr. George 
Hague, did much to make the building attractive. The 
members of the Microscopical Society exhibited slides 
during the afternoon, and Mr. Bert Shaw, one of our 


32 


members, gave pleasure to many with the gramophone. 
The orchestra was on hand, as usual, and the Ladies’ 
Committee served refreshments in the lecture hall. 

On Thursday evening, April 16th, the Social Commit- 
tee co-operated with the Camp Committee in the holding 
of a very enjoyable Camp Reunion. Views of the camp 
and different camping parties were shown by the stereop- 
ticon and a programme of songs and recitations was car: 
ried out, with refreshments at the close. 

The Reception Committee has been on duty with com- 
mendable regularity during the year. The building has 
seen an unusually large number of visitors this year, 
and the great number of young men coming from old 
lands to this country, place additional responsibility upon 
the committee in welcoming and extending the courtesies 
of the Association to strangers. 

Sunday Evening Strangers’ Tea. 

This tea is held each Sunday evening at 5.30 o’clock. 
The guests are introduced to each other and meet the 
officers and members, who endeayor to make them wel- 
come to the Association and its privileges. A half hour 
is then spent socially, closing with devotional exercises, 
after which the men are directed to the churches they 
may wish to attend for the evening services. The com- 
mittee and secretaries of the Association are constantly 
on the outlook for strangers. In this way they meet 
with those who take an interest in them, and the simple 
hospitality of the Sunday Evening Tea has led to wider 
acquaintance and friends in the Association Building. 
The expressions of appreciation by those who have at- 
tended the tea show that it is filling a large place in the 
work. Forty-eight sessions. have been held and three 
hundred and eighty-three men present. Of this number 
the following countries represented :— 

Oanadan 20 Sais Wales.

EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT. 


The committee have earnestly considered the need 
which exists among young men for supplementary educa- 
tion to compensate for lack of early schooling, to fit men 
for positions of greater responsibility, and to occupy lei- 
sure time to good purpose. They have endeavored to 
make a thorough study of our field during the year in 
order to meet the growing need for this kind of work in 
the city. At present our accommodation is entirely 
inadequate. Every available room in the building has 
been used during the season. Our equipment for com- 
mercial and technical subjects is not what it should be. 
More room is needed for mechanichal drawing, chemistry 
and physics. <A suitably equipped laboratory for the 
latter studies would be a great advantage. We are plan- 
ning to make the best use of the space available in the 
building next season. 

Courses of study in fifteen subjects were arranged 
and carried out by the committee during the term of 
twenty-five weeks from October 1st to March 31st. Four 
hundred and thirty-six different men were enrolled, an 
increase of seventy-seven over the preceding year. The 
total number of class enrolments was four hundred and 
ninety-eight. New classes were added in typewriting, 
architectural drawing and chemistry. The results were 
most satisfactory. Seventy-four students wrote on the 
International examinations at the close of the season, 
forty-seven of which were passed by the local examiners 
and their papers forwarded to the International Commit- 
tee for final marking. In addition, local examinations 
were held in elementary arithmetic, electricity and 
French by the teachers of these classes. 

The orchestra, under the leadership of Mr. Charles 
Reichling, has rendered valuable service on several occa- 
sions during the year.

A series of “ Practical Talks” was given during the 
winter season as follows :— 


Jan. 22.—* The Stock Exchange,” Mr. ©. E. Gault. 

Jan. 29.—“The Resources of our Country,’ Prof. T. 
W. Robertson (Department of Agriculture, Ottawa). 

Feb. 12.—‘* Advertising,” W. E. Desbarats (Desbarats 
Advertising Agency.) 

Inter socials were held, which greatly promoted social 
feeling among the students. 

A new feature this year was the formation of a meet- 
ing for Bible study, composed of students from the even- 
ing classes. Twenty-five men were enrolled and twenty- 
five sessions held with an average attendance of eleven. 

The Annual Closing took place on Thursday, April 
7th, an enjoyable social evening being spent with about 
one hundred men present. Addresses were delivered by 
Mr. C. T. Williams and Mr. Seth P. Leet, K. C.

Reading Room and Library Committee. 


The committee have sought to promote the more fre- 
quent and intelligent use of both the Reading Room and 
Library. In the Reading Room one hundred and sixty-one 
papers and periodicals are on file—one hundred and 
twenty-six purchased at a cost of two hundred and 
sixty-five dollars, and thirty-five donated. A return of 
$85.06 was realized at the annual sale in December. The 
following new magazines and papers have been added :— 
“Country Life in America,” “Ladies Home Journal,” 
“The Interior,’ “American Field,” “National,” “System,” 
“ Halifax Daily Chronicle.” 

We have the best reading room in the city, and, judg- 
ing by the way it is used, the members of the Association 
-and visitors appreciate it. 

While it is not possible to record accurately the num- 
ber using the Reading Room, a conservative estimate 
would be an average of three hundred daily. The com- 
mittee are considering the rearrangement of the room, 
which would greatly add to its attractiveness. 

In the Library some effort has been made by way of 
suggestion, to direct the reading of our members. Five 
reading courses on English history, Canadian history, 
natural history, the Far East and biography have been 
printed and circulated. While these have not been in use 
long enough to report definite results we believe it has 
been a wise move. We have purchased or had donated 
during the year one hundred and sixty-two books, as fol- 
lows : —

PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


Progress has been made in the character of the work 
of this department, and also in the esprit de corps of the 
men engaged in its different activities. 

Dr. H. B. Cushing was secured as an additional medi- 
cal examiner, and both he and Dr. F. W. Gilday have ren- 
dered most valuable service in the department, which the 
committee appreciate and desire to publicly acknowledge. 

Two changes were made last season in the gymna- 
sium curriculum :—The holding of a Junior Business 
Men’s Class, twice a week, at 6.15 o’clock. This class has 
been so successful that the committee feels warranted in 
continuing the same. The two main points of its success 
were the interesting of new young business men and the 
recalling of old members who had dropped out because 
no gymnasium classes suited them as to time. The other 
change was the moving of the advanced class to the same 
night as the intermediate class, thereby relieving the con- 
gestion of the floor caused by the elementary class and 
allowing them more time. This arrangement also pro- 
vided two extra hours per week during which the gymna- 
sium floor’ was free for general exercise, a thing greatly 
to be desired. 


359 


Throughout the year informal class socials were held 
at different intervals, which were found helpful in unit- 
ing the classes. 

The committee regret exceedingly that they are un- 
able to report progress in the matter of securing a larger 
accommodation for boys and intermediates, or the secur: 
ing of an athletic field. 

The committee desire to express their appreciation of 
the kind, courteous interest and conduct of the members 
in the welfare of this department. 

The class attendance is as follows :—

Total attendance for last year.. .. .. .. 18,985 


The elementary, students and business men’s classes 
show an increase over the previous year. 


The Junior and Boys’ classes show a decrease over 
last year, due to the change in membership fees. The 
total number registered in all the classes is 654 as 
against 631 last year. 

New members examined, men, 245 ; boys, 125. Total 
370. The re-examination of old members was greater 
this year than last. 


Leaders’ Corps. 


The corps consisted of twenty-four active members 
who co-operated with the Physical Director in the con- 
duct of the classes in the gymnasium. The Exhibition 
in the Gymnasium on New Year’s Day in which the Lead- 


40 


ers took a prominent part, was a success in every way. 
The eighth annual banquet of the Gymnasium Leaders 
Corps, March 12th, 1903, was the best ever held. The 
second annual banquet of the Physical Department Com 
mittee was held on April 27th. It was attended by 
about two hundred men and was a decided success. On 
the invitation of Mr. C. C. Holland an “At Home” was 
held at his residence where a most enjoyable evening was 
spent, and a sleigh drive was also held which was very 
well attended and thoroughly enjoyed, supper being serv- 
ed in the building. A photograph of members of the 
Corps is being made by Notman and the original will be 
presented to the Association. 

This has been one of the most pleasant and helpful 
years in the history of the Gymnasium Leaders Corps. 


Gymnasium Men’s Bible Study Club. 


The Club met every Sunday for thirty weeks and had 
for its year’s subject “ Important Decisions.” The thanks 
of the Club are due Mr. Frank Armstrong for the furnish- 
ing of remarkably fine advertising bulletins throughout 
the season. The Committee are certain that many gym- 
nasium men have been helped to a higher and better life. 
One hundred and twenty-five different men attended the 
class. The enrolment was 70. The total attendance for 
thirty sessions was 1,112, an average of 37. 


Tennis Club. 


The five double courts were in use both morning and 
evening as well as Saturday afternoons and_ holidays. 
Lady members were given the privilege of playing every 
day except Saturdays, up to five o’clock, and Tuesday and 
Saturday evenings. The Club entered the intermediate 
tournament composed of the following teams:—Montreal, 
McGill, St. Lambert, Lachine and Y. M. C. A. In the 
finals between ourselves and St. Lambert, St. Lambert 
won out, giving us second place. Membership numbered 
——. The past year has been the most successful one 
in the history of the club. The financial statement shows 
an even balance. 


41 


Cricket Club. 


The season of 1902 was a most enjoyable one and 
everything considered, fairly successful. It was practi- 
cally our first year in Montreal and District Amateur 
Cricket League, and the record of three matches won and 
six lost is nothing to be ashamed of. The club was great- 
ly handicapped owing to the want of suitable grounds. 
After paying all expenses a balance of $2.77 was turned 
in to the Association. At the close of the season a very 
pleasant dinner was held. 


Hockey Club. 


The Hockey Club had a very successful season, both 
in regard to the number of members, which was forty- 
five, and the games played. 

They entered a team in the Junior Hockey League of 
Canada which finished second in the section in which 
they were placed. This is very gratifying as the team 
was comparatively new, and considering that the other 
teams had been together for years, the boys feel justly 
proud of their work. The regular schedule of gaines 
was drawn up for the benefit of the members not haying 
a place on the representative team, but owing to several 
of our practice hours at the Arena being usurped by 
Senior League games, it was found impossible to finish 
the series. The club closed its year free of debt. 


Bowling Alleys. 


The last season was a most successful one for this 
club. It opened in October. A weekly competition was 
started on November 17th, giving a silver spoon for the 
highest single string each week, and a monthly competi- 
tion, giving a gold spoon for the highest average three 
strings made during the month. In April a closing com- 
petition was held giving a pearl pin for the highest three 
strings. All these competitions were very closely con- 
tested and the scores were high, the average for winning 
spoon being 2093. In January the club formed three 
teams and arranged a schedule of games to be played 
during the season. No. 3 team won out. In February 
a challenge came from Quebec Y. M. C. A. which we 


42 


accepted and managed to win out with the small margin 
of three pins. After the match the team treated the 
visitors to refreshments. A number of other outside 
games were played and, with one exception, the team won 
every time. Our financial statement shows a balance 
of $35.00 on hand. Our intentions towards improvements 
for the coming season are as follows:—To have the alleys 
planed and waxed, to get three new balls and to get four 
old ones turned, to get one new set of pins, to get one 
new return stop for the balls and to get new mattresses. 


Basket Ball. 


Basketball was popular this year, there being four 
senior and six intermediate teams of eight men each. The 
intermediate series was won by the “ Vics.” The 
“Maples” were the winners of the senior championship 
of the gymnasium as well as the city championship. 
There were about one hundred seniors and ninety juniors 
playing on teams. 


Athletic Club. 


Never before in the history of the Athletic Club has 
it had a more successful year. We had the use of the 
Montreal Baseball Park. Great interest was manifested 
in lacrosse, running, jumping, hammer throwing, etc. 
The club played two games of lacrosse, and though we 
suffered defeat in both cases, the boys showed that they 
had the making of a very good team. The average attend- 
ance at the grounds for three nights a week was twenty- 
seven per night. 

The Association Field Day was conducted for the first 
time by the members of the Athletic Club on the 17th of 
September, and was very successful. The events were 
run in proper time and order, and were closely contested. 
The prizes for the events were presented in the evening. 
We again thank the various donors to our Field Day 
Prize List for their kindly support. Our financial state- 
ment shows that we were able to assist the Field Day 
Committee with a cash balance of $7.83, and also to pre- 
sent to the ‘Association a framed photo of our Champion 
Track Relay Team. 


Baseball Club. 


On account of their being no baseball league in the 
city the interest was not as good as in former years. 
Only four regular games were played during the season. 
The club used the Montreal Baseball Park three evenings 
per week and had a membership of thirty-one. The aver- 
age attendance at practices was eighteen. Club closed 
year with a credit balance of $15.64. 


Snowshoe Club. 


This club, during the past winter, held ten tramps to 
different parts of the city. The average attendaice was 
thirty. This sport, which is purely Canadian, is becom- 
ing very popular in the city. The club hopes, next year, 
to be one of the best and largest in the city. It closed 
its session with all accounts paid. 


Summer Camp at Lac St. Joseph, Ste. Agathe. 


This popular feature of the Association has been car- 
ried on during the past year with the very best results to 
the Association as a whole. It provides an attractive 
and delightful vacation opportunity for our members at 
a reasonable cost, and is a strong social feature in the 
Association life. 

This work is handled by a Junior Committee who have 
charge of the Boys’ Camp from the middle of June to the 
12th of July, and by a Senior Committee who have in 
charge the balance of the season, from July 12th to Sept. 
ist. During the past year seventy-two boys spent their 
vacation here under the supervision of the Junior Com- 
mittee, from June 12th to July 12th, and 116 senior mem- 
bers, from July 12th to Sept. Ist. The total receipts from 
the Junior Camp were $519.73, expenses $453.76, leaving a 
balance of $65.97. The receipts from the Senior Camp 
were $1,331.87, and expenses $1,003.39, leaving a balance 
of $328.48. At the close of the season the two commit- 
tees handed over to the Permanent Camp Committee 
$398.05. The Permanent Camp Committee owed the 
Association for monies advanced, $437.87. They reduced 


45 


this amount by $200.00, leaving their indebtedness to the 
Association at the close of the year, $237.87. 

The Permanent Camp Committee require to expend 
about three hundred dollars each year in permanent 
improvements in order to keep up the equipment of the 
camp. The following improvements are now under con- 
sideration. A new range, two new boats, pump for con- 
veying water to the kitchen, new boat house and wharf. 

In connection with both the Junior and Senior Camp 
special religious services were held. The result of this 
work was most pronounced in connection with the boys’ 
section. Services were not only held on Sunday but dur- 
ing the week, and the committee in charge feel confident 
that a number of the boys were there led to take a stand 
for the first time in the Christian life. In connection 
with the Senior Camp services were held every Sunday 
morning and, whenever possible, special speakers were 
sent out from the city for this purpose, and each Sunday 
evening a song service was held. These were very much 
appreciated. In addition to this a song service and 
prayer meeting were held every Wednesday night. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


The work for boys was continued at three points during 
the year: The Central Building, North-East End, and 
Point St. Charles. 

The membership at the Central Building was:

The increase made in the fees at the Central Building 
of $1.00 for school boys, and $2.00 for business boys, and 
the fact that Evening Educational Classes for the latter 
had to be discontinued on account of lack of room, caused 
a decrease in the number of members. 


46 


Fifty-seven junior members renewed into the senior 
department. 

Fifty-three boys served on Committees. This affords 
an excellent opportunity for training for future service, 
and is‘of untold value to the boy. 

The Friday evening meeting had an average attend- 
ance of 31, and the afternoon meeting for junior school 
boys, of 27, the total average being 58. One of the results 
of the Summer Camp was an increase in the attendance at 
the evening meeting during July and August. Illustrated 
talks were given—one by Rey. Clifford Ascah, on Christian 
Life and work at a Hudson Bay post, and the other by Mr. 
Kristen Borup on Mission life and work in Uganda. The 
attendance at these was 168 and 154 boys. 

Twenty boys expressed a desire to lead the Christian 
life during the year. 

In Bible study definite progress was made. Seven 
group classes were held each week during the winter, with 
a total membership of 44. 

The Hospital services were continued every second 
Sunday morning, with an average attendance of 28. The 
boys from the branches were well represented. 

Special services were held on Christmas and Easter. 
These services are very greatly appreciated by both the 
patients and the hospital staff. 

The Reading Room and Library continued to be an 
attractive feature to the members. This department re- 
quires constant additions of new books. Donations of 
suitable books, or money to purchase the same, are earn- 
estly solicited. 

The following social features were held : Three recep- 
tions for new members in the fall months, three socials 
for the members of the three gymnasium classes, the 
annual tea for the committee members, the tea for the 
members of the different Bible classes, the Camp Re-union, 
a sleigh-drive, the gymnasium opening and closing even- 
ings, and the closing entertainment at which a report of 
the work was given by lantern slides. In addition to these 
features several “outings” were held during the summer. 

The gymnasium classes were attended as follows :

Two monthly competitions were held in each class, for 

which prizes’ were awarded. The interest in Basket ball 
yas as great as evyer—4 teams in the senior school boys, 

5 teams in the junior, and 7 teams in the business boys’ 
tournaments, made things interesting. At the close of the 
basket ball season gymnasium hockey was played by the 
two school boy classes, and proved very attractive. 

Seven snowshoe tramps were held. 

SuMMER CAmp.—This feature grows in interest with 
the boys. It was held in two sections: 


Business Boys, June 12 to 26....23 Attended 
School Boys June 26 to 12...... 41 Attended 


Mr. John Brown had charge of both camps, supported 
by an excellent corps of tent leaders. Camp life in all its 
delights was most enthusiastically entered into by all the 
boys, and they all returned without an accident. 

The spiritual life of the camp was, as usual, a very 
strong feature. The Friday evening meetings and Friday 
services left a lasting impression upon the boys, and a 
number can date their start in the Christian life from the 
1902 Summer Camp. 

The North East Branch was in charge of Messrs. C. 8. 
Paterson, W. E. Cushing, D. M. Black, R. L. Charlton, 
Frank Jarvis and Gordon Elliott, assisted by McGill 
students. This committee rendered most unselfish service. 
The house at 72 Mitcheson Street was suitably furnished 
with books, games, etc., and it was kept open three nights 
each week. A hockey club was formed. Religious meet- 
ings were held on Friday and Saturday evenings. The 
committee has no hesitation in recommending that a suit- 
able building be erected for boys in that section. 

The Point St. Charles Branch continued the Friday 
night meeting with interest and profit to the boys in that 
section. The members of the committee were: Messrs. 
R. B. Ross Jr., E. C. Budge, T. C. Felgate, E. U. Howell, 
W. S. Swaill, and James Ross. The new building will 
afford an opportunity for doing an enlarged work for the 
boys of that section. 


A. L. PATERSON, Chairman.

RAILROAD DEPARTMENT—Point St. Charles. 


The regular work of this department has been almost 
entirely suspended owing to the inadequacy of the pre- 
sent building for such work. Sunday afternoon meet- 
ings have been held as usual. The new building is now 
under construction and is expected to be ready for occu- 
pation in October next.

The Ladies’ Auxiliary of the Montreal Branch has 
continued its work with Mrs. Mingie, as president, Miss 
Shotten as treasurer, and Miss N. A. Collins as secretary. 
They have decided to endeavor to raise five hundred dol- 
lars towards the furnishing of the building. Towards 
this amount twenty-five dollars has been realized from a 
lecture by the Rev. M. Webb. Collection books are being 
distributed to work for the balance. Their treasurer’s 
statement shows a balance in hand of $54.95. 


THE LADIES’ COMMITTEE. 


“The Ladies’ Committee assists in the social work and 
looks after the furnishing of the parlors. The committee 
is able to do this work through the kindness of its contri- 
butors, the ladies of the various churches having respond- 
ed very kindly at all times to requests for money or sup- 
plies for the socials, or for assistance in serving refresh- 
ments. <A constitution was drawn up and adopted and 
the committee organized in the form of a Ladies’ Auxili- 
ary. All ladies who contribute $1.00 or more to the work 
annually are considered members. From the list of 
members, the directors appoint the Executive Committee. 
This Executive, in turn, meets and elects officers and 
appoints the various committees to carry on the work. 
At present there are five sub-committees, viz., Finance, 
Membership, Social, Flower, Furnishing and Junior, con- 
sisting of from three to seven members each. 

Open meetings were planned for, from time to time, 
to give the members of the Auxiliary the opportunity of 
showing what work is being done and how the money is 
being spent. We also wish to give our members an insight 
into the general work of the Association. 


Social. 


We have provided for a reception given to Mr. Fred. B. 
Smith on the occasion of his visit to the city, the New 
Year’s reception, a supper to the Hockey Club, a banquet 
for the closing of the physical classes, and the annual tea for 
the Committee Men, also assisted at the Strangers’ Tea and 
other social occasions. 


Furnishing. 


Thus far our work has been limited to the assisting 
at social occasions and, to some extent, in keeping the 
furnishing of the parlors as attractive as they should be. 
We have also supplied table linen, dishes and cutlery. We 
gratefully acknowledge the gift of several dozen hand- 
some cups» and saucers from one of our warmest friends, 
Mrs. John W. Ross, and wish that such an example were 
found worthy of imitation. 


Flowers. 


The mission of this committee is primarily to supply 
flowers for any of the members, who may be sick. When 
we remember that at such times the majority of young 
men are either in the hospital or in boarding houses, we 
can realize what pleasure a few flowers and kind wishes 
bring. Thanks are due to Mrs. Reford, one member of 
our committee, who has been most generous with her 
greenhouse all through the winter. Over thirty young 
men have received this attention during the past season. 
Another part of our work is to send a few cut flowers to 
the building every Saturday. These serve to brighten 
the rooms and make them appear more homelike. 


Junior. 


This committee assists by serving refreshments at the 
close of the evening’s entertainment for the reception of 
new members in the fall. During the winter a series of 
small gatherings are held, a few boys at a time, and at 
these some of the committee are present helping to sup- 
ply the social element, while once a year all the boys who 
serve on any committee, about seventy-five of them, sit 
down to tea together, which our committee serves, and 
afterwards discuss their work. Last fall we assisted the 
North East Branch of the Boys’ work in the furnishing 
of their rooms. Through a grant of twelve dollars from 
the Ladies’ Committee, we were enabled to put new cur- 
tains and other furnishings in the boys’ rooms in the cen- 
tral building.

Name and 
Object. 


Basis. 


Membership. 


Constitution of the Association as Revised and Adopted, April 28th, 1903. 


YOUNG MEN’S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION 
OF THE 


CITY OF MONTREAL. 


CONSTITUTION. 
ARTICLE I. 


Sec, 1. The name of this Society shall be “The Young Men’s 
Christian Association of the City of Montreal.” 

Sec. 2. The object of this Association shall be the improvement 
of the spiritual, intellectual, social and physical condition of young 
men and boys over 12 years of age. 


ARTICLE II. 


Sec.1 This Association seeks to unite those young men, who, 
regarding Jesus Christ as their Lord and Saviour, according to the 
Holy Scriptures, desire to be His disciples in their doctrine and in 
their life, and to assocate their efforts for the extension of His 
Kingdom among young men. 

Sec, 2. This Association adopts as the basis of all its proceed- 
ings those fundamental principles of Evangelical Christianity on 
which all orthodox Protestant churches are agreed, and will never 
admit any intermeddling with those matters of faith and polity on 
which such churches differ. 


ARTICLE III. 


Sec. 1. The members of this Association shall be young men 
eighteen (18) years of age or over, and boys twelve (12) years ot 
age or over. Members shall be classed as Active and Associate. 

Sec. 2. Any young man who is a member in good standing of a 
Protestant Evangelical Church, according to the evangelical test* 


*Norr.—‘And we hold those churches to be evangelical which, 
maintaining the Holy Scriptures to be the only infallible rule of faith 
and practice, do believe in the Lord Jesus Christ (the only begotten 
Son of the Father, King of Kings, and Lord of Lords, in whom 
dwelleth the fullness of the Godhead bodily, and who was made sin 
for us though ,knowing no sin, bearing our sins in his own body on 
the tree), as the only ‘name under heaven, given among men, where- 
by we must be saved’ from everlasting punishment.’’—Definition at 
International Convention, Portland, Me., 1869. 


55 


may become an Active member by election as hereinafter provided, 
and on payment of the membership fee, as prescribed by the rules 
of the Association. None but Active members eighteen (18) years of 
age and over shall have the right to vote or hold office. 

Sec. 3. Any young man with satisfactory references as to char- 
acter and general conduct may become an Associate member by elec- 
tion as hereinafter provided, and on payment of the membership fees, 
as prescribed by the rules of the Association. Associate members 
shall be entitled to all the privileges of Active members except the 
right of voting and holding office. 

Sec. 4. Members may be elected at any regular meeting of the 
Board of Directors, or Committee of Management of a Branch 
Association, by a majority vote of the members present, on the 
report of the Membership Committee of the Association or Branch. 

Sec. 5. Any active or Associate member may become a life 
member by the payment of $100.00 towards current expenses at any 
one time. 

Sec. 6. Honorary members may be proposed in writing to the 
Board of Directors at any of its regular meetings, and elected by a 
unanimous vote of the members of the Board present at such regular 
meetings. 

ARTICLE IV. 


Sec. 1. The members of this Association shall seek out young 
men, resident or strangers in Montreal and suburbs, and endeavor 
to bring them under moral and religious influences; aid them in 
selecting boarding-places and means of employment; introduce them 
to the members and privileges of the Association; secure their 
attendance at some place of public worship on the Sabbath ; by 
every means possible surround them with Christian influences, and 
by personal effort try to win them to Christ. 

Sec. 2. The members of this Association owe their first duty to 
the churches to which they respcetively belong. They shall seek to 
interest the churches to which they belong in the work and welfare 
of the Association. 

Sec. 8. They shall labor to induce all suitable young men of their 
acquaintance to connect themselves with the Association, and use all 
practicable means for increasing its membership, activity and use- 
fulness. 

ARTICLE V. 


Sec. 1. The general objects of this Association shall be carried 
out under the management of a Board of Directors of twenty-one 
members, elected from among the Active members of the Associa- 
tion, not more than one-third of whom shall be members of any one 
denomination. 


Duties ot 
Members. 


Management 


Sec. 2. There shall be an election of seven Directors by ballot ‘Annual 
at the Annual Meeting, who shall hold office for three years, or until Election, 


their successors are elected. 

Sec. 3. The Committee on Vacancies, at the March Board Meet- 
ing, shall report the names of persons to fill the places of those 
Directors whose terms of office expire. The names thus reported, 
if approved by the Board, shall be posted in the Association at least 
twenty days before the Annual Meeting, and submitted to the As- 
sociation for ballot at the ensuing regular election. Other nomina- 
tions for Directors may be made by any five Active members, such 
nomination to be made in writing to the General Secretary at least

of Directors

of Board.

ten days before the Annual Meeting. These nominations shall also 
be posted in the Association, and submitted for ballot at the Annual 
Meeting. 

Sec. 4. Vacancies occurring in the Board of Directors during the 
year, by resignation or otherwise, shall be filled as follows:—The 
Vacancy Committee shall present nominations at the next regular 
meeting of the Board, when an election by ballot shall take place to 
fill the unexpired term. 


Sec. 5. The Board of Directors at their first meeting succeeding 
the Annual Election shall elect by ballot one of their number to be 
President, one to be Vice-President, one to be Recording-Secretary, 
and one to be treasurer of the Association ; said officers shall hold 
office for one (1) year, or until their successors are appointed at this 
meeting. There shall also be appointed a General Secretary. 


Sec. 6. The Board of Directors shall have power to elect fifteen 
(15) Advisory Directors, who shall be members in good standing of 
Protestant Evangelical Churches, not more than five (5) from any 
one denomination. They shall be notified of all meetings of the 
Board of Directors, and shall have the right to attend and participate 
in the discussion of all matters brought before the Board, but shall 
not be entitled to vote. Such Directors, when elected, shall be 
divided into three classes, which shall hold office respectively, one 
(1), two (2), and three (8) years. Upon the expiration of such‘ 
terms respectively, the successors of those whose terms of office 
expire shall be elected by the Board of Dirctors for a term of three 
(3) years. 

ARTICLE VI. 


Sec, 1. The Board of Directors shall have and exercise all the 
powers conferred by the Act of Incorporation and by-law. 


Sec, 2. The several officers named in Section 5, Article V, shall 
have the powers to perform the duties incumbent upon officers of 
like name in similar Associations, subject to such by-laws and regu- 
lations as may be provided by the Boards of Directors. 


Sec, 3. The Board of Directors shall have the power to make 
and adopt such rules and by-laws for their government, the govern- 
ment of the Association, and of the Branches, not inconsistent with 
this Constitution, as they may deem expedient. 


Sec. 4. The Board of Directors shall hold their meetings at least 
once a month, except July and August, and seven shall constitute a 
quorum. Should a quorum not be present at the time fixed by the 
rules for any regular meeting of the Board, the members present 
may adjourn to another time, and any business which could be 
transacted at such regular meetings may be transacted at such ad- 
journed meeting. 

Sec, 5. The real estate or immovable property of the Association, 
as well as all funds of the Association, from whatsoever source de- 
rived, shall be held in its corporate name, and be managed and 
administered by the Board of Directors. 

Sec. 6. The Board of Directors shall have the general super- 
vision and control of the work and policy of the Association in all 
its details. All Secretaries and other employees are to be employed 
and controlled as may be determined by the Board of Directors. No 
contract, debt, or obligation shall be binding unless contracted by 
virtue of a resolution of the Board of Directors. 


57 
ARTICLE VII. 


Sec. 1. There shall be an Annual Meeting of the Association in 
the Month of May, when the reports of the Board of Directors and 
Treasurer shall be presented. 

Sec. 2. Meetings of the Association may be called by the Board 
of Directors at such time and place as they may determine. 

Sec. 3. Meetings of the Association may be called by the Presi- 
dent upon the written request of ten (10) Active members, the object 
of the meeting being specified in notice of the same, and no business 
may be transacted at such meeting except that for which the call is 
issued, 

Sec. 4. Twenty-five (25) Active members shall constitute a 
quorum at all meetings of the Association. 

Sec. 5. All meetings of the Association shall be opened by read- 
ing the Scripture and Prayer. No motion of a sectarian or political 
character shall be entertained by the Association. 


ARTICLE VIII. 


Sec. 1. As the best interests and the effectiveness of the Asso- 
ciation depend upon the activity of its members, the works of the 
Association shall be divided into departments, under the supervision 
of Committees appointed by the Board of Directors. The Board of 
Directors shall have the right to appoint special Committees for 
special purposes, and to define the duties and jurisdiction of the 
Committees of the departments, and of special Committees. 


ARTICLE IX. 


Sec. 1. No organization shall be effected within or in connection 
with the Association or any branch thereof, except by the sanction 
of the Board of Directors or Committee of Management of such 
Branch, and all such organizations shall be under the control of 
the Board of Directors or said Committee, and their Constitution, 
By-laws and Rules shall be approved by said Board or Committee. 
The Board of Directors shall have power to over-rule any action 
of any such organization which they may deem detrimental to the 
interests of the Association. 

Sec. 2. The Board of Directors or members of the Committee 
of Management shall be members ex-officio of such organizations. 

Sec. 8. The Board of Directors or Committee of Management 
shall have power to reorganize or disband any such organization. 


ARTICLE X. 


Sec. 1. The Board of Directors may, at such times and places as 
they may deem advisable, establish Branches or discontinue the 
same. These branches shall be under the entire control of the 
Board of Directors, under such regulations as the Board may from 
time to time adopt. 

Sec. 2. Each Branch shall be managed by a Committee of Man- 
agement, appointed by the President of the Association. subject to 
the approval of the Board of Directors, consisting of eleven or more 
Active members of the Association of whom a majority shall not be 
of any one denomination.

Committees.

tions,

58 


ARTICLE XI. 


Sec. 1. The Board of Directors or Committee of Management 
snall have power to deal with any cases of misconduct on the part 
of any member or persons visiting the rooms or meetings of the As- 
sociation or Branches, and have power to cancel his membership and 
to debar said person from all the privileges of the Association. 


ARTICLE XII. 


Sec. 1. The provision of this Constitution, by which none but 
members in good standing of evangelical churches shall be eligible 
for election to Active membership, as before mentioned, shall never 
be annulled, and no amendments to this Constitution shall be made 
which would allow the said provision to be annulled. 

In other respects this Constitution may be altered or amended 
by a vote of two-thirds of the Active Members present and voting 
at any business meeting of the Association provided such alterations 
or amendments shall have been submitted in writing to the Board 
of Directors, and subsequently posted in the Association for a period 
of not less than thirty days previous to the said meeting. 


ARTICLE XIil. 


Except as provided in the Act of Incorporation of the Association 
and its amendments, all former Constitutions are hereby repealed 
and set aside, and this Constitution shall take effect from this date, 
to wit, the 28th April, 1903, and all By-laws now in force which are 
not contradictory thereto or which may be authorized by the fere- 
going Constitution are, and shall remain in force until otherwise 
dealt with.
